title: The Reformed grant that faith makes one pleasing to God
source_text: XLV. Nec propterea tamen Schola Reformata negat id quod Romana gratiae gratum facientis nomine intelligit, fidem, scilicet, spem & charitatem esse aliquid cujus ratione homo Deo gratus & placens est singulari quodam modo, ad quem respiciens Paulus ad Hebraeos dicit, Impossibile esse sine fide placere Deo. Quo spectant Theologi Ecclesiae Romanae, dum gratiam istam gratum facientem appellant.
pass_a_gloss: XLV. Nor yet on that account does the Reformed School deny that what the Roman understands by the name of grace making pleasing, namely faith, hope and charity, is something by reason of which man is pleasing and acceptable to God in a certain singular way, looking to which Paul to the Hebrews says, It is impossible without faith to please God. To which the Theologians of the Roman Church look, when they call that grace making pleasing.
pass_b_english: Thesis XLV. Yet the Reformed school does not therefore deny that what the Roman school means by grace that makes pleasing, namely faith, hope and love, is something on account of which a person is pleasing and acceptable to God in a special way.

Paul has this in view when he says to the Hebrews that without faith it is impossible to please God, and the theologians of the Roman Church have the same in view when they call that grace the grace that makes pleasing.
